{{Short description|Inequality in information theory}}

In [[information theory]], the '''Bretagnolle–Huber inequality''' bounds the [[total variation]] distance between two probability distributions <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> by a concave and [[bounded function]] of the [[Kullback–Leibler divergence]] <math>D_\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q)</math>. The bound can be viewed as an alternative to the well-known [[Pinsker's inequality]]: when <math>D_\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q)</math> is large (larger than 2 for instance.<ref name="canonne">{{cite arXiv |last1=Canonne |first1=Clément |date=2022 |title=A short note on an inequality between KL and TV |class=math.PR |eprint=2202.07198}}</ref>), Pinsker's inequality is vacuous, while Bretagnolle–Huber remains bounded and hence non-vacuous. It is used in statistics and [[machine learning]] to prove information-theoretic lower bounds relying on [[hypothesis testing]].<ref name="bandit_algs" >{{cite book |last1=Lattimore |first1=Tor |url=https://tor-lattimore.com/downloads/book/book.pdf |title=Bandit Algorithms |last2=Szepesvari |first2=Csaba |date=2020 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |access-date=18 August 2022}}</ref> ([[Concentration inequality#Bretagnolle–Huber–Carol inequality|Bretagnolle–Huber–Carol Inequality]] is a variation of Concentration inequality for multinomially distributed random variables which bounds the total variation distance.)

== Formal statement ==

=== Preliminary definitions ===
Let <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> be two [[probability distribution]]s on a [[measurable space]] <math>(\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{F})</math>.
Recall that the [[total variation]] between <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> is defined by 
: <math> d_\mathrm{TV}(P,Q) = \sup_{A \in \mathcal{F}} \{|P(A)-Q(A)| \}.</math>

The [[Kullback–Leibler divergence]] is defined as follows:
:<math>D_\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q) = 
\begin{cases}
\int_{\mathcal{X}} \log\bigl(\frac{dP}{dQ}\bigr)\, dP & \text{if } P \ll Q, \\[1mm]
+\infty & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
</math>
In the above, the notation <math>P\ll Q</math> stands for [[absolute continuity]] of <math>P</math> with respect to <math>Q</math>, and <math>\frac{dP}{dQ}</math> stands for the [[Radon–Nikodym derivative]] of <math>P</math> with respect to <math>Q</math>.

=== General statement ===
The Bretagnolle–Huber inequality says:

: <math> d_\mathrm{TV}(P,Q) \leq \sqrt{1-\exp(-D_\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q))} \leq 1 - \frac{1}{2}\exp(-D_\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q)) </math>

== Alternative version ==
The following version is directly implied by the bound above but some authors<ref name="bandit_algs" /> prefer stating it this way.  
Let <math>A\in \mathcal{F}</math> be any event. Then

: <math>P(A) + Q(\bar{A}) \geq \frac{1}{2}\exp(-D_\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q))</math>

where <math>\bar{A} = \Omega \smallsetminus A</math> is the complement of <math>A</math>.

Indeed, by definition of the total variation, for any <math>A \in \mathcal{F}</math>,

: <math> \begin{align}
Q(A) - P(A) \leq d_\mathrm{TV}(P,Q) & \leq 1- \frac{1}{2}\exp(-D_\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q)) \\
& = Q(A) + Q(\bar{A}) - \frac{1}{2}\exp(-D_\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q))
\end{align}
</math>

Rearranging, we obtain the claimed lower bound on <math>P(A)+Q(\bar{A})</math>.

== Proof ==
We prove the main statement following the ideas in Tsybakov's book (Lemma 2.6, page 89),<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Tsybakov |first=Alexandre B. |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/b13794 |title=Introduction to nonparametric estimation |series=Springer Series in Statistics |date=2010 |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/b13794 |isbn=978-1-4419-2709-5 |s2cid=42933599 |oclc=757859245}}</ref> which differ from the original proof<ref name=":1">{{Citation |last1=Bretagnolle |first1=J. |chapter=Estimation des densités : Risque minimax |date=1978 |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/bfb0064610 |title=Séminaire de Probabilités XII |pages=342–363 |series=Lecture notes in Mathematics |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-540-08761-8 |access-date=2022-08-20 |last2=Huber |first2=C.|volume=649 |doi=10.1007/bfb0064610 |s2cid=122597694 |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> (see C.Canonne's note <ref name="canonne" /> for a modernized retranscription of their argument).

The proof is in two steps:

1. Prove using Cauchy–Schwarz that the total variation is related to the [[Bhattacharyya distance|Bhattacharyya coefficient]] (right-hand side of the inequality):

:: <math> 1-d_\mathrm{TV}(P,Q)^2 \geq \left(\int \sqrt{PQ}\right)^2</math>

2. Prove by a clever application of Jensen’s inequality that

:: <math>\left(\int \sqrt{PQ}\right)^2 \geq \exp(-D_\mathrm{KL}(P \parallel Q))</math>

* Step 1:

: First notice that

: <math>d_\mathrm{TV}(P,Q) = 1-\int \min(P,Q) = \int \max(P,Q) -1</math>

: To see this, denote <math>A^* = \arg\max_{A\in \Omega} |P(A)-Q(A)|</math> and [[without loss of generality]], assume that  <math> P(A^*)>Q(A^*)</math> such that <math>d_\mathrm{TV}(P,Q)=P(A^*)-Q(A^*)</math>. Then we can rewrite

:: <math>d_\mathrm{TV}(P,Q) = \int_{A^*} \max(P,Q) - \int_{A^*} \min(P,Q) </math>

: And then adding and removing <math>\int_{\bar{A^*}} \max(P,Q) \text{ or } \int_{\bar{A^*}}\min(P,Q)</math> we obtain both identities.

: Then

:: <math> \begin{align}
1-d_\mathrm{TV}(P,Q)^2 & = (1-d_\mathrm{TV}(P,Q))(1+d_\mathrm{TV}(P,Q)) \\
& = \int \min(P,Q) \int \max(P,Q) \\
& \geq \left(\int \sqrt{\min(P,Q) \max(P,Q)}\right)^2  \\
& = \left(\int \sqrt{PQ}\right)^2 
\end{align}
</math>

: because <math>PQ = \min(P,Q) \max(P,Q). </math>

* Step 2:

: We write <math>(\cdot)^2=\exp(2\log(\cdot))</math> and apply [[Jensen's inequality]]:
:: <math> \begin{align}
\left(\int \sqrt{PQ}\right)^2 &= \exp\left(2\log\left(\int \sqrt{PQ}\right)\right) \\
& = \exp\left(2\log\left(\int P\sqrt{\frac{Q}{P}}\right)\right) \\
& =\exp\left(2\log\left(\operatorname{E}_P \left[\left(\sqrt{\frac{P}{Q}}\right)^{-1} \, \right] \right) \right) \\
& \geq \exp\left(\operatorname{E}_P\left[-\log\left(\frac{P}{Q} \right)\right] \right) = \exp(-D_{KL}(P,Q))
\end{align}
</math>

: Combining the results of steps 1 and 2 leads to the claimed bound on the total variation.

== Examples of applications ==

=== Sample complexity of biased coin tosses ===
Source:<ref name="canonne" />

The question is 
''How many coin tosses do I need to distinguish a fair coin from a biased one?''

Assume you have 2 coins, a [[fair coin]] ([[Bernoulli distribution|Bernoulli]] distributed with mean <math>p_1=1/2</math>) and an <math>\varepsilon</math>-biased coin (<math>p_2=1/2+\varepsilon</math>). Then, in order to identify the biased coin with probability at least <math>1-\delta</math> (for some <math>\delta>0</math>), at least 
:<math> n\geq  \frac{1}{2\varepsilon^2}\log\left(\frac{1}{2\delta}\right).</math>

In order to obtain this lower bound we impose that the total variation distance between two sequences of <math>n</math> samples is at least <math>1-2\delta</math>. This is because the total variation upper bounds the probability of under- or over-estimating the coins' means. Denote <math>P_1^n</math> and <math> P_2^n</math> the respective joint distributions of the <math>n</math> coin tosses for each coin, then

We have
:<math> \begin{align}
(1-2\delta)^2 & \leq d_\mathrm{TV}\left(P_1^n, P_2^n \right)^2 \\[4pt]
& \leq 1-e^{-D_\mathrm{KL}(P_1^n \parallel P_2^n)} \\[4pt]
&= 1-e^{-nD_\mathrm{KL}(P_1 \parallel P_2)}\\[4pt]
& = 1-e^{-n\frac{\log(1/(1-4\varepsilon^2))}{2}}
\end{align}
</math>
The result is obtained by rearranging the terms.

=== Information-theoretic lower bound for ''k''-armed bandit games ===
In [[multi-armed bandit]], a lower bound on the minimax regret of any bandit algorithm can be proved using Bretagnolle–Huber and its consequence on hypothesis testing (see Chapter 15 of ''Bandit Algorithms''<ref name="bandit_algs" />).

== History ==
The result was first proved in 1979 by Jean Bretagnolle and Catherine Huber, and published in the proceedings of the Strasbourg Probability Seminar.<ref name=":1" />  Alexandre Tsybakov's book<ref name=":0" /> features an early re-publication of the inequality and its attribution to Bretagnolle and Huber, which is presented as an early and less general version of Assouad's lemma (see notes 2.8). A constant improvement on Bretagnolle–Huber was proved in 2014 as a consequence of an extension of [[Fano's Inequality]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gerchinovitz |first1=Sébastien |last2=Ménard |first2=Pierre |last3=Stoltz |first3=Gilles |date=2020-05-01 |title=Fano's Inequality for Random Variables |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1214/19-sts716 |journal=Statistical Science |volume=35 |issue=2 |doi=10.1214/19-sts716 |arxiv=1702.05985 |s2cid=15808752 |issn=0883-4237}}</ref>
